# **~~BME’s  COPPER B~~ RIEFING** **~~S~~ ERVICE** 

## **October 2009** 





#### **CFTC Actions to Support Copper?** 

**_Copper trading higher, with Dollar support prices CFTC pressure on oil and grain could help copper Supply disruption improves market tone .....but demand prospects are lowered Market to remain in surplus until Q2 2010_** 

**_Downward price move overdue in the near term_** 

After trading at around $6,000/t early in the month, LME cash moved sharply upwards from mid‐month, settling at around $6,500/t. The main reason for this price trend appears to have been a renewed fall in the US Dollar. Copper, for now, is acting as a currency hedge. 

Longer term, a rebalancing of books by index‐linked investors following CFTC action on oil and grain could prove very positive for copper. In August, exemptions to position limits on grain by two index operators were revoked. The CFTC is now engaged in a review of the influence of commodity indices on oil and grain pricing. There are some signs that the funds are already moving away from these products, fearing tighter position limits and disclosure rules. 

The focus on oil and grain is not by accident. The pricing of both is highly sensitive politically. In 2008, escalating food prices led to the spectre of food riots. An oil price hike is disliked as, not only do high oil prices affect every day existence in higher fuel prices, earlier hikes are closely associated in with deep recession and a shift in geopolitical influence to OPEC countries. Against this, very high copper prices are quite benign. 

While there are positives, there is little in the physical market to support high prices. Current economic data are mainly positive, but at this stage in the cycle we should be very worried if this were not the case. We note a slowing in month‐on‐month gains in the global economy from July, and signs of worsening business and consumer confidence in Europe and North America. 

Sluggish growth in refined copper consumption confirms the economic data. This, of course, is with the exception of China, where consumption appears to have picked up quite strongly in September. A surprise 23% monthly rise in refined copper imports into China in September against no arbitrage led to confidence that China still needs more copper, despite huge imports earlier this year. But, too much should not be made of this. Spot copper in China is trading at a discount to Shanghai, indicating a lack of buying interest, and copper imported 

now may have been booked three months ago. In coming months we are concerned that current booming construction could lead to another property bubble. A huge excess of floor space being constructed over that being sold is, we believe, unsustainable. While China’s consumption growth set to moderate, in Europe and the United States, fabricators are indicating less bullish prospects for 2010 than we had assumed. Also, the market will be hit by higher scrap use.

###### **Copper Cathode Trading Higher, Despite Exchange Stock Rise** After trading below $6,000/t on most days at the end of September and early in October, a sharp upward trend in LME Cash started mid‐month. This took the cash price up to near $6,700/t (October 26th). The market has remained in cash‐to‐three‐month contango, by $20‐35/t. Prices further out followed Cash and 3‐month prices, the forward curve remaining fairly flat. The upward trend in prices had no encouragement from visible stocks. The amount of copper in LME warehouses continued to rise, by around 30 kt in the past four weeks. There has also been a small rise in the amount of material on Comex and Shanghai. The rise in LME stocks was mainly in South Korea and Europe. Exchange stocks in Europe, however, remain at levels that may prove critical should demand pick up strongly. Blister Market Balance

###### **Spot Premia Stable or Weakening** The Codelco producer premium for European delivery was unchanged at $80/t, keeping the relatively low level set a year earlier, but $35/t lower than it had been previously. This comparatively light premium reflects the realities of the physical market. Although exchange stocks are scarce, very little is booked for delivery and demand remains weak. The spot premium, at around $50‐60/t this month, is low, having slipped by $5‐15/t compared to the previous month. In the United States, the New York dealer premium remains largely unchanged, although the trading range is large. For large tonnages with a long lead time, consumers can achieve 3.0‐3.5 c/lb over spot Comex, delivered Midwest. Some recent deals are rumoured to have been at US$10/t and 1.0 c/lb and lower, with some business done at zero and zero. Annual TC/RC negotiations are about to start. Smelters are expected to start their offers at US$60/t and 6c/lb, citing higher production costs and low acid revenue The mines, on the other hand, will be looking for numbers at or below the recent mid year settlements, citing the current and likely continuing tightness in th

ll around 6% lower now than it was last year, a time when output was already sliding. The sluggish pace of recovery places some doubt on the common assumption that the recovery will be “V‐ shaped”. Despite having raised its forecasts for 2010 by 0.6%, the IMF still forecasts a modest 3.1% global economic growth next year. Significantly, the rate of pick‐up in mature economies is expected to be very modest indeed. The IMF forecasts 1.7% growth in Japan, 1.5% in the United States and only 0.3% in the Euro region. In October, the Conference Board’s index of consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since July, slipping to 47.7 from 53.4 in the previous month. The exact reason for the weak data is not clear, as manufacturing output up to September was on a rising trend and unemployment falling; perhaps the pace of recovery is just too slow to convince consumers that better times really are round the corner. In Europe, also, confidence is weak, although it had been improving until September. The German ZEW index of analyst and investor sentiment for October is worrying, having fallen after three months of gains. Lower exports from Germany (and the rest of Europe) is thought to be behind the worsened sentiment. China, in contrast, seems to be doing better and better. ### **Consumption Trends** Understanding the physical copper market right now depends on getting China right. Clearly, a vast amount of copper has gone into the country this year. It is not so clear how much of this is for consumption. Estimates for the year to date range by as much as one million tonnes. We estimate that Chinese refined copper use in the past nine months is up by 17% on last year. Reported semis data indicate a 19.9% rise in output. This would imply a larger increase in refined copper use, as direct melt scrap use has diminished. A much higher consumption figure is derived taking into account copper output, net imports and known stock increases. This gives a rise of 37.2%. Clearly, there has been considerable stock build in China, so the reported semis figure looks more realistic. We believe that this figure is also too high, as it has been in recent years. Our lower figure is in line with end market trends. Although some sectors are doing very well, including automotive and (recently) construction, the market is marred by reduced exports of OEM goods and a fairly low rate of growth in power cable output. In Europe, the United States and Japan, fabricators report slowly improving business, but from a very low base. KME, in Europe, reported a 30% year‐on‐year decline in the first half of 2009, and expects the second half to be 20% down on last year. Luvata,

er in concentrates from the market. It could also impact on refining capacity if the current running of Olympic Dam processing plant at sub‐optimal levels causes damage. Deeper production cuts could result from strikes. The strike at BHP’s 200 ktpy Spence is showing no immediate sign of resolution, talks two weeks into the strike having stalled. BHP did manage a deal at the much larger Escondida mine, but it was more generous than other miners (including Codelco) seem prepared to offer. Maybe because of Escondida, workers at Codelco’s 220 ktpy Andina mine have reversed their initial willingness to accept a 3% wage increase plus bonus. They now want a 5% wage hike plus bonus. Codelco has looming the end‐year expiry of labour contracts at Chuquicamata and Radomiro Tomic, together accounting for 800 ktpy of mine supply. In Peru, the final outcome of talks around the expired contract at BHP’s 330 ktpy Antamina mine remains uncertain. In Canada, output losses continue as a result of the now‐longstanding strike at Vale’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay, still showing no sign of resolution. In the United States, however, there appears to be no willingness to strike, despite the high copper pricing. Labour deals have successfully been brokered at Kennecott Copper. ###### **Renewed Appetite for Investment** Given the high copper prices, unsurprisingly there is a renewed appetite for investment. Codelco has been helped to secure its ambitious programme, mainly aimed at reviving older mines by securing US$1 billion in funding from government. Private investors are also advancing low risk mine extensions, amongst them Xstrata’s Lomas Bayas and Freeport McMoran’s El Abra projects, both in Chile. Longer term, companies are beginning to publicise greater ambition for their position in copper in the future. Anglo American recently stated that it may double its copper output to 1.3 million tonnes by 2017. For the short term however, caution remains. In a recent interview, the CEO of Freeport stated that idled mine capacity would not be reactivated until there are definite signs of renewed copper demand in Europe and North America. He did, however, also state that plans for reactivation were being drafted. Kt Cu % Concentrates

A secondary haulage shaft, able to lift ore to the surface at 20‐25% of the rate of the main shaft, is now in operation. The company expects the mine to be back to full production by end‐ March 2010. In the interim, the integrated flash smelter and anode furnaces will operate at greatly reduced rates due to lack of feed material. South Korean state‐run mining company **Kores** agreed in 2008 to invest US$200 million in Corocoro, giving it a 45% share. Copper output of 30‐50 ktpy is anticipated. _Thomson Reuters, October 28th 2009._ **Botswana: Discovery Metals Ltd.** plans to raise an initial US$150 million to fund development of its **Boseto** project. A feasibility study is due to be complete early in 2010, with first production slated for mid‐2011. The project is expected to produce 25 ktpy of copper and 691 kozpy of silver. _Thomson Reuters, October 8th 2009._ **Canada: Vale** has re‐commenced partial operation at its **Sudbury** nickel‐copper complex, re‐starting at **Clarabelle Mill** and resuming mining at **Coleman Mine 153** and **Garson Ramp** . Codelco’s investments are intended to stem a loss of market share resulting from falling output at its ageing mines. The bill also brought changes to the structure of Codelco to reduce political influence and thus enhance competitiveness relative to private mining companies. _Platts, October 7th 2009._ Union workers called a strike on October 13th at the **Spence** mine after rejecting **BHP Billiton’s** final offer of a single 4% pay rise over a two year contract plus around US$15,000 in bonuses. The labour union had been demanding a 5.5% increase and US$20,000 in bonuses. The Spence electrowon processing unit is currently operating at about one‐quarter utilisation rate, sufficient to maintain its technical integrity. The mine has nameplate capacity of 200 ktpy, and in 2008 produced 165 kt of copper cathode. _Thomson Reuters, October 16th 2009 & October 22nd 2009._ A strike was averted at the giant 990 ktpy **Escondida** mine when workers accepted an offer from **BHP Billiton** of 5% wage increase over the 44 month contract with bonuses and benefits to each worker worth around US$25,000. The offer was higher than that made to **Spence** workers for their contract of shorter duration. _Thomson Reuters, October 13th, 2009._ Workers at **Andina** mine rejected an early proposal by **Codelco** for a 3% wage increase and around $16,000 in bonuses and benefits. The Andina labour contract expires on November 30th. The labour union has put in its demand for a 5% wage increase and benefits linked to productivity over the life of the two‐year contract. **Barrick Gold Corp** has purchased **Xstrata’s** 70% interest in the **El Morro** copper‐gold project for US$465 million. The project, estimated to cost US$2.5 billion, is expected to produce 150 ktpy of copper and 300 kozpy of gold over fourteen years. Construction should take 2 ‐3 years. _Mining Journal, October 12th, 2009._ 

**Xstrata Copper** is to develop **Fortuna del Cobre** in northern Chile in order to extend the mine life of its adjacent **Lomas Bayas** SX‐EW mine by eight years to 2020 at 75 ktpy. The **Lomas Bayas II** project will cost US$293 million. _Platts, October 15th 2009_ 

**Freeport‐McMoran** plans to resume **Sulfolix** project to extend the life of **El Abra** mine by ten years to 2020, at a cost of US$600 million. The initial phase should be completed by 2012 and cost US$450 million. The project will involve the mining of sulphides once the oxide resource is depleted. El Abra produced 168 kt of copper in 2008. _Thomson Reuters, October 7th, 2009._ 

Repairs have been completed at the control room powering the main conveyor belt at **Xstrata** / **Anglo American’s Collahuasi** mine. The company initially estimated on July 27th that the damage would reduce ore extraction by around 20 kt during a two month repair period. Repairs were completed on September 14th. _Thomson Reuters, September 30th 7th, 2009._ 

**Cochilco** (Chilean Copper Commission) predicts that in the period 2009—2015 investments in Chilean copper mining could be US$39.5 billion. This would increase output from 5.3 Mt copper in 2008 to 7.4 Mt by 2020 (of which 5.7 Mt would be in concentrates). _Thomson Reuters, October 14th, 2009_ **.**

There is no sign yet that negotiations regarding KMT are due to re‐commence. **Russia: Urals Metals & Mining Co.** has postponed until 2012‐2014 its plan to increase the capacity of its **Uralelectromed** refinery by 37% from 380 ktpy to 500 ktpy. The company had earlier planned to carry out the capacity increase in 2010. The plan requires a US$31.4 million investment in a new electrolysis workshop. _Thomson Reuters October 16th 2009, Marchmont News October 14th 2009._ 

**Jiangxi People Wire & Cable Co., Ltd.** has started to construct an RMB 110 million (US$16 million). MV power cable plant able to produce cables up to 35 kV. The project is located in **Shangrao City** . _Aintake, October 1st 2009._ 

**Shuanglong Metals Industry Co., Ltd.** has started construction of a 25 ktpy copper semis and 12 ktpy stainless steel tube facility in **Yingtan City** , Jiangxi. The private company was established with an investment capital of RMB 200 million (US$29 million). _Aintake, October 1st 2009._ 

**Zambia:** The **Chambishi** smelter plans to double its blister processing capacity to 300 ktpy in 2010 following an increased requirement for processing capacity in the region. **Kansanshi** , a unit **of First Quantum** , and **Chibuluma** , owned by **Metorex** , has recently joined **Equinox Minerals' Lumwana** mine in using the Chambishi smelter. The Chambishi smelter is a JV between **China Non‐ferrous Metals Corporation** (CNMC) and **Yunnan Copper** . It had initially been used to treat copper from **NFC Africa** , a subsidiary of CNMC. _Thomson Reuters, October 19th 2009._ 

**Japan: Nippon Mining & Metals** is to expand production of its proprietary HS1200 rolled copper foil to a commercial level. The product is unusual in that it contains tin (0.12%), adding to strength, but retains an electrical conductivity of 90%. The main application of the foil is in lithium ion batteries for electric and hybrid cars. _Japan Metal Bulletin, October
